prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant topological insulators, and the experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B050 as my single-part position, unchanged in configuration from round 1. The round-1 exchange tested it from every side and the scientific core held: Kane and Mele showed that spin-orbit coupling alone, without a magnetic field, can give a time-reversal-protected insulator with conducting edge channels and a Z2 invariant, which is a new organising principle for band insulators, and Molenkamp's group measured the predicted quantised edge conductance in HgTe/CdTe wells. Both the prediction and the decisive measurement are in hand, and roughly two decades of independent transport and ARPES work in several material families mean maturity is not in question. The chair's summary shows that no member disputes this; the open points are credit and overlap, and I think both can be answered in the citation. On overlap with 2016, that prize recognised topological phase transitions and Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz physics, whereas a symmetry-protected state in a time-reversal-invariant band insulator with no net field was not inferable from that work, and the citation should say what is new rather than invoke 'topology' generally. On the 2D versus 3D question, I would anchor on the quantum spin Hall effect because that is where the prediction and the confirming experiment are a matched pair, and keep downstream uses such as computational screening of topological materials out of the citation; that is a consequence of the discovery, not a part of it. Three names, one coherent achievement and no more than the limit allow.
statement.case_against: The attribution objection has not gone away and I will not pretend that it has. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe quantum-well route that told Molenkamp where to look, and Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth each called that omission a real defect, in Lindroth's words a defect in the prize itself. The three-dimensional contributors (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore and Balents; Hasan's group) are also outside the credits, and 3D materials arguably had larger materials impact than the 2D effect. The 2016 overlap remains a fair concern for the Academy even if I think it answerable. Against B051 specifically, I concede that Katori and Ye is the cleanest credit on the shortlist and that the clock is at least as mature as B050; I rank it below B050 only because I weigh a new organising principle above a new level of accuracy, and that is a judgement of criterion, not of scientific quality.

responses.point: Lindroth says the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission is a defect in the prize itself, not a footnote, and that she would not oppose B050 if the committee can settle the credit.
responses.response: I take this as the strongest statement of the attribution problem and I accept it as a real cost. Where I land differently is on what the committee can settle. Under a three-person ceiling, the question is whether the prediction of the effect (Kane and Mele) and its first observation (Molenkamp) are the achievement being credited, or whether the HgTe proposal is. I read the first as the achievement, because Kane and Mele predicted the effect and the quantised edge conductance in HgTe is its direct confirmation, whereas BHZ identified the material platform in which it would appear. I would not swap Mele for BHZ, since Mele is a co-originator of the Z2 insulator, and I would not swap Molenkamp, since without the measurement this is a prediction rather than a discovery. So I keep the trio and would record in the citation that the prize is for the effect and its observation, and not for a materials recipe. That is a choice with a price, and I accept that you may weigh the price differently.

responses.point: Kroll argues that B051 has a defect-free credit because Katori and Ye cover both the proposal and the record-performance realisation, and that the magic-wavelength condition is a new principle distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
responses.response: Your argument on novelty is persuasive and I have moved on it: after reading your reply to Olsson and Lindroth's reply to you, I accept that the magic-wavelength lattice is a different principle from the comb or from single-ion control, and I no longer treat the 2005 and 2012 overlap as the main weakness of B051. It also helps that you and Lindroth would not make a prize wait for the SI redefinition. My remaining difference is the criterion you posed in the summary. A symmetry-based classification that reorganised how a whole class of materials is understood and computed seems to me to carry more conceptual reach than an improvement in accuracy, even a spectacular one with a many-body-limited error budget. I would not call that a decisive argument against B051, and I would accept it as the winner if the committee gives weight to clean attribution over breadth. That is why I keep B051 first among my alternatives.

responses.point: Johansson argues that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission leaves out a decisive theory contribution, that distance from the 2016 prize is unclear, and that B050's broad support does not make it better science than trapped-ion computing.
responses.response: I agree with the last point: support counts are not a substitute for scientific judgment, and I do not rest on them. My case for B050 over B015 is scientific. B050 has a prediction and a measurement of a defined observable, both confirmed repeatedly, whereas for B015 you yourself list three weaknesses: the Wineland 2012 overlap, an experimental third name that is partly arbitrary, and no demonstrated scalable machine. I accept your argument that a computing architecture is a different intellectual contribution from the measurement and control of single quantum systems; I do not think the overlap is disqualifying. But the Blatt-versus-Wineland-versus-Monroe credit seems to me harder to defend than the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp credit, even with the BHZ question. On 2016, the Z2 invariant and time-reversal-protected edge states were not part of the cited work, and I would ask you which feature of the 2016 citation you think reaches them.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that DFT-based screening is downstream use and should carry no weight in the citation, and that a theory-only Kane-Mele prize would lose the confirmation that makes the case compelling.
responses.response: I agree on both points and I am glad you pressed the first. The computational screening of topological materials is a consequence of the discovery, and as someone who does that work I should be especially careful not to let it enter the case; the citation should name the prediction and the HgTe observation only. On the theory-only fallback, I agree that dropping Molenkamp would remove what turns a prediction into a discovery, so I do not treat it as a good fallback. If the BHZ issue were judged fatal, I would prefer to move to a different prize, such as B051, rather than to a Kane-Mele-only version of this one.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang under the three-name ceiling; I judge it defensible but with a real cost, and if the committee rules otherwise I would move to B051.

Whether the 2016 prize is judged distinct enough; I think the Z2 time-reversal-protected state is a separate achievement, but Johansson and Mehlig remain unsure and the Academy may read it differently.

Whether the committee should weight conceptual reach (B050) over a clean credit and metrological precision (B051); this is a criterion choice on which I could be outvoted without the science being wrong.
I am relying on my own recollection of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu-Kane and HgTe priority history and have not verified details.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no documented link to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye or the MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer group. My field, theoretical condensed matter including electronic-structure methods used to screen topological materials, is close to B050 and I have kept that downstream work out of the case; this is field proximity and not a recusal issue. I chaired the 2025 cycle, whose subject was different. I note the disclosures of Johansson (recusal from B038), Kroll and Lindroth, and Olsson's Chalmers tie to Johansson, and none bears on my position.
